items.title: Headlines for November 16, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## U.S. Air Travelers Continue to Face Canceled or Delayed Flights After Nationwide Ground Stop Order Nov 16, 2026 U.S. air travelers continue to face canceled or delayed flights today after a weekend of travel chaos sparked by a nationwide ground-stop order that halted domestic flights for about four hours on Friday. It was the biggest disruption to U.S. air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks. More than 12,000 flights were canceled throughout the weekend; thousands more faced delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy refused to apologize for the cancellations during several public appearances. Duffy blamed a contractor doing maintenance to upgrade old copper wire to fiber-optic cable, and also blamed the travel chaos on prior presidential administrations and called on Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to modernize air traffic control systems. Democrats pointed to $12.5 billion already approved by the Republican-controlled Congress for Department of Transportation upgrades and said the Trump administration had only spent about $1 billion of those funds. Meanwhile, two people were injured on Saturday night when two planes collided on the tarmac while taxiing at Miami International Airport. ## Iran Launches Attack on Bahrain, Targeting Radar Positions Nov 16, 2026 Iran launched an attack on Bahrain early Sunday, the latest strike on the kingdom, as clashes between Iran and the U.S. continue while peace talks remain stalled. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted radar positions at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base with six drones. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. Bahrain is officially home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, though the Pentagon largely abandoned its base there after it was heavily damaged by Iranian attacks in the opening days of the U.S. war on Iran. In recent weeks, U.S. forces have quietly hit several Iranian targets, among them Qeshm Island, which houses a major Revolutionary Guard naval facility. This is Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson. > Esmail Baghaei: “We will not leave any attack unanswered. No military aggression against Iran by the United States or others will go unanswered. We have demonstrated this in practice, and we will continue to act in the future in whatever manner and by whatever means Iran’s powerful armed forces deem appropriate.” ## Yemeni Government Forces Retreat to Defend Aden from Houthis Nov 16, 2026 In Yemen, forces aligned with the internationally recognized government announced Sunday they were retreating from areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait in order to focus on defending their interim capital, Aden. It’s a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against fighters with the Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis. The retreat came as Houthi forces pushed to within 40 miles of Aden. Meanwhile, the International Committee of the Red Cross said Sunday the Houthis had unilaterally released hundreds of prisoners. This is the head of the Houthis’ prisoner affairs committee. > Abdul Qader al-Murtada: “The largest and most extensive amnesty and release operation has been carried out. This operation includes 600 detainees who were captured over the past years, all of whom were captured on the frontlines, particularly along the border battle fronts. Most of them have been in captivity for several years, and some are individuals with humanitarian needs, including the ill and the elderly.” ## Mass Funeral Held in Gaza for Dozens of Palestinians Killed by Israeli Forces Nov 16, 2026 In Gaza, a mass funeral was held Sunday for dozens of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces and whose remains had been trapped in the rubble for years. Palestinian officials in Gaza say 70 skeletal remains were found beneath what were once homes and underneath the ruins of destroyed buildings in Gaza’s north. At least 10 of them were children. The remains of an estimated 8,000 Palestinians are believed to still be trapped in the rubble after more than three years of Israel’s war, and as Israeli forces block the entrance of heavy equipment needed to properly search for the missing in Gaza. Gaza has been described as the “world’s largest mass grave.” This comes as a senior Hamas commander, Samir Abu Younis, was killed in an Israeli strike on Khan Younis Saturday. Dozens of Palestinians attended his funeral Sunday. ... ## NYT: Israel Abducted Two Iranian Generals in Effort to Locate Missing Israeli Air Force Navigator ... A New York Times investigation has found that Israel abducted two Iranian generals in recent years in a bid to gather intelligence about the 1986 disappearance of Israeli Air Force navigator Ron Arad in Lebanon. Both generals were secretly interrogated by Israel’s spy service Mossad. One of them, Alireza Asgari, was abducted in Turkey in 2006 and killed after his interrogation. The other general, Abdullah Saberi, was kidnapped in Damascus, Syria, in 2021 and later released in Johannesburg, South Africa. He said he had been tortured by his Israeli captors. The kidnappings came despite multiple Israeli intelligence reports that concluded Iran had not been involved in the missing airman’s disappearance. ... ## Democrats Win Governor’s Race in Alaska Nov 16, 2026 Democrats have won Alaska’s governorship for the first time since 1998. Former state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins beat three Republicans, one of them endorsed by Donald Trump. His win gives Democrats control of 30 governorships nationwide. Meanwhile, in Alaska’s Senate race, Democrat and former Congressmember Mary Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 3.7 percentage points, or just over 10,000 votes. ## Death Toll from U.S. Measles Outbreak Rises to 10 Nov 16, 2026 The death toll from the measles outbreak in the U.S. has jumped to at least 10, as more infections erupt across several states. Wisconsin health officials reported the death of a child Friday, marking the second measles-related death in the state so far this year. On the same day, officials in Pennsylvania said an unvaccinated resident had died of measles. This comes as the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization revoked the designation amid an unprecedented measles outbreak nationwide with more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases this year. The rapid spread of measles cases comes as Trump’s Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has backed anti-vaccine policies.

items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 16, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including a joint call by Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK on Israel to allow urgent humanitarian aid into Gaza, the reported deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and the interception of drones over Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions with Yemen's Houthis. The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom urged Israel to "stop the delays now" and permit the immediate entry of 150,000 tents and critical supplies into Gaza ahead of winter. "We ... are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire," the top diplomats said in a joint statement. Noting that recent flooding from the first winter storm has compounded civilian suffering, the ministers warned that border restrictions are blocking desperately needed shelter and relief materials. They stressed that the crisis remains "entirely reversible" before harsher weather sets in, calling on Israel to open border crossings and grant entry to "dual-use items" required for humanitarian operations and early recovery "before it is too late."

items.title: U.S. inflation report highlights strain of rising food, energy and housing costs | PBS News Hour Classroom
items.excerpt: ### SUMMARY High inflation persisted last month, providing little relief for Americans struggling with affordability. It is driven largely by food and energy price increases, but housing costs also rose. The country appears to be headed for an annual inflation rate of about 4% this year. To discuss what it means for the economy, Geoff Bennett spoke with Austan Goolsbee of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.

items.title: Grocery inflation is set go up as input costs rise
items.excerpt: Conditions are ripe for grocery inflation to rise at a relatively fast clip over the coming months as persistently high energy costs and rough climate conditions pose challenges for food producers and retailers, Ricky Volpe, professor of agribusiness at California Polytechnic State University, said Thursday during a briefing hosted by FMI — The Food Industry Association. The high price of diesel and the start of an El Niño weather pattern that meteorologists expect to be especially powerful are likely to disrupt supply chains, putting upward pressure on food prices and pushing up food-at-home prices at a faster-than-average pace at least into early 2027, Volpe said. "There's not a whole lot that's moving in the right direction in terms of keeping food prices flat or down right now … it would surprise me to see food prices go flat or trend down in the next four or five months," he said. The Producer Price Index, which tracks wholesale prices and provides clues about the future direction of retail prices, has been rising in recent months, with costs for transportation, commodities, energy and storage all going up, Volpe noted. Volpe pointed to palm oil as an example of an essential ingredient in foods including baked goods and cereals that could become more expensive because of El Niño, as parts of the world that are major producers of the commodity are likely to see ... Grocery inflation has bumped around on a month-to-month basis in 2026 but rose last month at the fastest pace since April, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported last week. Volpe noted that the 0.4% jump in grocery inflation recorded in October was "pretty substantial," adding that if the metric increased at that rate every month for a year, it would translate into a 5-percentage-point boost on an annual basis. The BLS did not report year-over-year figures for inflation last month because it did not capture data for the same period in 2025 due to the federal government shutdown.

items.title: Economic Update: Week of November 16, 2026
items.excerpt: ## Growth Real GDP grew 3.4% SAAR in 3Q, accelerating from 2.2% in 2Q and exceeding expectations, as strong business investment and consumer spending outweighed a drag from net exports. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, while nonresidential investment surged 12.7%, supported by continued AI-related spending. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, and federal spending added nearly 1% to growth, while residential investment fell 3.3% amid demographic shifts and high mortgage rates. Looking ahead, growth may moderate as fiscal support fades and housing remains weak, though business investment should continue to provide support. Imports of AI-related hardware may keep net exports a drag, but with PCE inflation at 3.6%, the Fed may look to raise rates in December. ## Jobs The October jobs report showed payrolls rising by 165k, well above expectations of 70k, while August and September payrolls were revised higher by a combined 84k. Hiring was driven by professional and business services, health care and transportation and warehousing, helping private-sector payrolls rise by 159k. Government employment was relatively muted, adding just 6k jobs. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, while wage growth came in above expectations at 3.1% year-over-year, though it remained below headline inflation for the seventh consecutive month. For the Fed, a strengthening labor market leaves more room to focus on inflation. ... ## Inflation Headline CPI rose 0.4% m/m, driven in part by higher food and energy prices. Core CPI again came in hotter than expected, rising 0.3% m/m compared to expectations of 0.2%. Core inflation was led higher by several categories, including shelter, transportation services and medical care, while used car and truck prices provided some relief. With this being the final CPI report before the December meeting, the core reading strengthens the case for further tightening, with the size of the next move increasingly in focus. ## Rates At its September meeting, the Federal Reserve voted 10-2 to maintain the federal funds rate target range at 3.75-4.00%. The committee upgraded its growth assessment to “strong” from “solid,” but also noted the need for more information to assess the impact of last month’s rate hike, preserving the option to hike or hold in December. Economic strength outside of AI was also highlighted while the committee reaffirmed its commitment to returning to 2% inflation. Although markets are pricing in a December hike, upcoming inflation data will be key in determining whether it materializes.

items.title: Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid Says Inflation Remains Too High | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Miriam Hart Nov 16, 2026, 7:29 PM UTC ... U.S. inflation remained above the Federal Reserve’s 2% objective, and Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City President Jeff Schmid said Sunday that reducing price growth had become more difficult since August. He made the remarks at the National Credit Union Management Association 2026 Conference in Kohala Coast, Hawai’i. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% from a year earlier in September, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported. The index excluding food and energy increased 3.1% over the same period. For the month, the overall index rose 0.5% and the core measure gained 0.3%. Schmid cited a 5.7% annualized rise in consumer price index (CPI) prices over the three months through October. That is a three-month pace, not a year-over-year rate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said October CPI rose 0.4% from the previous month, seasonally adjusted. It did not publish a 12-month rate because October 2025 comparison data were unavailable after a lapse in federal appropriations. Schmid described the labor market as largely balanced, with wage growth around 3% and about one available job for each job seeker. He pointed to higher oil costs, tariffs, demand tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure and rising health care expenses as sources of price pressure. Employer health-benefit costs, he said, had risen more than 6% over the past year, their fastest pace in more than 20 years. For durable goods, Schmid said prices advanced 2.9% in September; only the pandemic-era surge exceeded that increase in the period since 1987. Schmid said durable-goods prices fell year after year from 1995 to 2020. New York Fed President John Williams voiced a similar concern on Nov. 12, saying inflation remained above the Fed’s goal; EconoTimes previously covered Williams’ warning on inflation. Schmid said supply disruptions can have a greater effect on prices when demand is strong, while the Fed can influence demand. “Demand always plays a role in inflation,” he said. His prepared remarks did not recommend a specific interest-rate move. The BEA’s October Personal Income and Outlays report, which includes PCE data, is scheduled for Nov. 25 at 8:30 a.m. EST.

items.title: Live updates: Trump heads to Asia ahead of meeting with Xi, Putin in China
items.excerpt: November 16, 2026, 6:48 PM EST ... ## What to know today - TRUMP'S ASIA TRIP: President Donald Trump departed Washington today for a pair of summits this week in the Philippines and China, where he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss nuclear disarmament issues and the Iran war, the White House said. - NVIDIA SUCCESSION: Trump told reporters this morning that he “would not mind” if Jensen Huang were reinstated as CEO of Nvidia after he resigned following allegations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. - GUN BAN CHALLENGE: The Supreme Court this morning declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland’s restrictions on people carrying firearms in a broad range of public areas. ... ## Another Democratic lawmaker receives letter from DOJ official over potential congressional oversight A fourth Democratic member of Congress has been targeted by a Justice Department official over post-midterms remarks about congressional oversight. U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz today posted a letter addressed to Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to chair the House Oversight Committee next year, writing that Garcia had “openly declared your plan to target citizens associated with the President.” “A committee gavel is not a prosecutor’s commission,” Reitz wrote. “You cannot say that the investigations you fantasize about are confined to a lawful legislative end.” Garcia's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Reitz’s letter. Reitz sent letters to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., suggesting their rhetoric could run afoul of federal law. Earlier today, Reitz indicated to NBC News that more letters to Democratic lawmakers could be coming. “I’ve got people that are looking at what certain key leaders have said, and then I’ll make the judgment call whether it warrants a demand letter in individual cases,” Reitz said. Under DOJ protocol, this type of overt action against sitting members of Congress would require clearance from the Public Integrity Section of the Justice Department. That office has been gutted in Trump’s second term, and is down to two attorneys. White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Garcia last week warning him that “threats” to launch congressional investigations into the administration could be a crime. In response to Scharf’s letter, Garcia said in a statement: “It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate.” ... ## John Thune says Trump administration has $8 billion in unspent money for air traffic control upgrades Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters today that the Trump administration has $8 billion at its disposal for air traffic control upgrades. Thune said that $12.5 billion in funding was passed through legislation, of which only about $4 billion has been spent. He added that although he agreed modernizing and updating systems was needed, senators have questions about the administration’s request for $50 billion in additional funding following Friday’s nationwide ground stop. “I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority,” Thune said. “But also, we want we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we’re using taxpayer dollars wisely and well. So, we’ll hear them out and see what the questions are.” ... ## Supreme Court rejects challenge to Maryland’s ‘sensitive places’ gun ban The Supreme Court this morning declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland’s restrictions on people carrying firearms in a broad range of public areas. The court for now sidestepped a chance to define what exactly is a “sensitive place,” a term used in previous rulings to describe locations where guns could be banned. As a result, the Maryland restrictions remain in place. The Supreme Court this morning rejected Trump’s move to abruptly cancel academic funding for researchers in California because his administration deemed the projects to be inconsistent with policies such as his opposition to diversity initiatives. The court left in place lower court rulings that said the government violated the free speech rights under the Constitution’s First Amendment by terminating grants issued to University of California researchers. ... ## Sen.-elect Scott Colom says investing in the South can help Democrats win ‘a durable majority’ Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats need to invest more in Southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped a seat blue for the first time in decades. “What we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur,” he said yesterday. Colom’s projected win this month brought Democrats to a 55-seat majority in the Senate, with Alaska’s Senate race yet to be called. His victory over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, marked a seismic political shift in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago and has not had a Black senator since the Reconstruction period.

items.excerpt: As Democrats gear up for substantial majorities in Congress, one question looms: who will take the helm? So far, no one has challenged Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for the House speaker role. Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is setting his sights on unseating longtime leader Chuck Schumer in the Senate. - 🎧 A wave of incoming senators has spent months hearing voters demand change in Washington. NPR's Eric McDaniel says this presents a real opportunity for Van Hollen and a potential risk for Schumer, especially after the recent election results. Van Hollen needs 30 Democrats to secure a simple majority. He has support he needs from popular progressives like Bernie Sanders, and incoming members like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, McDaniel says. Since votes are cast by secret ballot, it's uncertain how many will back each leader when they convene in a few weeks, and McDaniel says anything could happen.

items.excerpt: - AP - Nov 16, 2026 - Nov 16, 2026 Updated 55 mins ago Robert Pattinson is named the 7th James Bond, taking over from Daniel Craig Robert Pattinson has been unveiled as the next James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to play the iconic British spy and the first since Amazon MGM took over the beloved film franchise. The naming of Pattinson on Monday comes during the longest hiatus in 007 history and ends years of rampant speculation about who would inherit the role from Daniel Craig. Pattinson described getting to play Bond as “the honour of a lifetime.” Denis Villeneuve, who will direct the next film, praised Pattinson as having “a timeless soul.” Pattinson only entered the Bond rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role. Others reportedly in the mix included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult. Raye leads 2027 Grammy nominations, followed by Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Rodrigo and more NEW YORK (AP) — The Recording Academy announced the 2027 Grammy Award nominations on Monday, with English singer-songwriter Raye leading the pack. She's up for 11 awards, including record, song and album of the year. This ties Beyoncé’s record for the most nominations in a single year by a woman artist. Raye’s album “This Music May Contain Hope” has earned her critical acclaim. Spanish singer Rosalía follows with nine nominations, while Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers each have seven. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026’s best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each. The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 on ABC, Disney+, and Hulu. Glenn Close marvels at honorary Oscar as Ridley Scott and indie producers also get statuettes LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close has finally received her first Oscar, an honorary award at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles. Close, 79, was honored alongside director Ridley Scott, animator Floyd Norman, and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler. Close, who has been nominated eight times without a win, expressed deep gratitude for the recognition. John Malkovich, her “Dangerous Liaisons” co-star, presented the award, praising her remarkable career. Matt Damon honored Ridley Scott, who accepted via video. The event, which often kicks off Hollywood’s awards season, also celebrated Vachon and Koffler's contributions to independent cinema and Norman's groundbreaking work in animation. Grammy nominations snub Harry Styles and hip-hop, while surprises include Dolly Parton NEW YORK (AP) — The 2027 Grammy Award nominees have been announced, sparking inevitable discussions about snubs and surprises. Notably, there's no hip-hop in most general field categories, a shift from last year. Women dominate many major categories, with only Bruno Mars breaking the trend. Harry Styles did not receive a nomination and Noah Kahan only received one. Beyoncé makes history with her 100th career nomination. Dolly Parton and Tim Curry receive posthumous nominations. A new category for Asian pop music performance has been introduced, but BTS chose not to participate and thus wasn't nominated. The awards will air on Feb. 7. Gérard Depardieu drops appeal and accepts sexual assault conviction PARIS (AP) — French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set. He will accept the 18-month suspended sentence and has issued an apology. Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 for groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” in 2021. The court ordered him to pay fines and list his name in the national sex offender database. Depardieu acknowledged his past behavior and decided to withdraw his appeal. He is expected to face other legal proceedings soon.

items.excerpt: ##### Rosalía makes Latin Grammy history with third Album of the Year win Rosalía stole the show at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, winning five awards, including her third Album of the Year title. The Spanish superstar also claimed Song of the Year and Best Pop Song for “ La Perla”, alongside Best Alternative Music Album and Best Short Form Music Video for “ Sauvignon Blanc”, making her the night's biggest winner. ##### Azerbaijani film wins top prize at international festival in The Hague Azerbaijani short film “ The Dance of Triumph” has claimed the top prize in the Global Peace, Harmony and Human Rights category at the 2026 International Film Festival The Hague. Written and directed by Garay Hasan, the film tells the story of a war veteran who lost both legs and is struggling to rebuild his life while keeping a promise to a fallen friend. A 13-member jury unanimously chose the film as the winner, praising its compelling storyline, strong performances and outstanding aesthetics. The festival attracted 503 submissions, with 63 films from 23 countries chosen for the final programme. ##### Philippines makes history with first Eurovision Asia victory The Philippines has made history after winning the first-ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia, held in Bangkok, Thailand, where 11 countries competed for the title. Singer Carmelle, 19, secured the historic victory with her women’s empowerment anthem “ Sobra-Sobra”, scoring 211 points – 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote. Thailand’s MANG x DAOU took second place with 170 points. ##### Johnny Depp tops box office for first time in eight years with 'Ebenezer' Johnny Depp has returned to the top of the North American box office for the first time in eight years, with his latest film, “ Ebenezer”, debuting at No. 1. The Charles Dickens-inspired production brought in an estimated $19 million in North America and $23 million internationally, taking its worldwide opening earnings to $42 million. Directed by Ti West, the film drew mixed reviews, scoring 52 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes. Audiences, however, responded more positively, with 65 per cent of ticket buyers saying they would definitely recommend it to friends. ##### Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman honoured with Oscars Hollywood icons Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman were presented with honorary Oscars at the 17th Governors Awards in Los Angeles on Sunday, celebrating their outstanding contributions to cinema. The ceremony also marked a historic first, as Killer Films co-founders Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler became the first all-female producing team to receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.
